Local LLM Setup on M3 Max (llama.cpp + Hugging Face)

Overview

  • Run open-source LLMs locally on M3 Max 36GB
  • Stack: llama.cpp for inference + hf CLI for model downloads
  • Exposes OpenAI-compatible API → drops into Codex, OpenCode, Aider, Continue
  • Claude Code support via LiteLLM proxy (Anthropic ↔ OpenAI translation)
  • MLX is a faster alternative for raw throughput — see Alternative Runtimes
  • Analogy: llama-server is to local LLMs what Postgres is to local DBs — a daemon you point clients at

Default Model: Qwen3.6-27B

  • Top pick for 36GB as of Apr 2026
    • 27B dense, ~16GB at Q4_K_M
    • Beats prior-gen Qwen3.5-397B-A17B on coding benchmarks
    • 262k native context (extensible to 1M)
    • Apache 2.0
    • GGUF community quants already published

Setup Steps

1. Install both tools

brew install llama.cpp hf
  • llama.cpp ships with Metal enabled by default on macOS
  • hf is the renamed HuggingFace CLI (was huggingface-cli)

2. Authenticate with Hugging Face

hf auth login
  • Token from https://huggingface.co/settings/tokens
  • Required for gated models (Gemma, Llama) — also accept license on the model page in browser first

3. Download a model (GGUF format)

  • Coding default — Qwen3.6-27B (~16GB):

    hf download unsloth/Qwen3.6-27B-GGUF \
  Qwen3.6-27B-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  --local-dir ~/models

  • General — Gemma 3 27B (~16GB):

    hf download bartowski/gemma-3-27b-it-GGUF \
  gemma-3-27b-it-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  --local-dir ~/models

  • Quant cheat sheet for 36GB:

    • Q4_K_M → default, best size/quality tradeoff
    • Q5_K_M → +25% size, slight quality bump
    • IQ4_XS → smaller, near Q4_K_M quality (uses imatrix)
    • Q8_0 → near-lossless, only viable for ≤14B models

4. Run the server (OpenAI-compatible API)

llama-server \
  -m ~/models/Qwen3.6-27B-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  -ngl 99 \
  -c 16384 \
  --flash-attn on \
  --cache-type-k q8_0 \
  --cache-type-v q8_0 \
  --port 8080
  • Endpoint live at http://localhost:8080/v1
  • Critical flags:
    • -ngl 99 → all layers on GPU (Metal). Always set this
    • --flash-attn on → ~30% speedup, lower memory (use on|off|auto, no longer a bare toggle)
    • --cache-type-k/v q8_0 → halves KV cache memory
    • -c 16384 → 16k context (KV cache scales linearly, only bump if needed)
    • --mlock → optional, pins model in RAM, prevents macOS swapping

5. Wire into agentic coding tools

OpenCode (recommended — native OpenAI-compatible, no proxy)

  • Install: 
    npm install -g opencode-ai
# or: brew install sst/tap/opencode
  • Configure ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json: 
    {
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "provider": {
    "local": {
      "npm": "@ai-sdk/openai-compatible",
      "name": "Local llama.cpp",
      "options": {
        "baseURL": "http://localhost:8080/v1",
        "apiKey": "dummy"
      },
      "models": {
        "qwen3.6-27b": {
          "name": "Qwen3.6 27B (local)"
        }
      }
    }
  }
}
  • Run: opencode → use /models to pick local/qwen3.6-27b
  • Quick env-var alternative (no config file): 
    export OPENAI_BASE_URL=http://localhost:8080/v1
export OPENAI_API_KEY=dummy
opencode

Codex / Aider (also OpenAI-compatible)

export OPENAI_BASE_URL=http://localhost:8080/v1
export OPENAI_API_KEY=dummy

Claude Code (needs Anthropic ↔ OpenAI proxy)

pip install 'litellm[proxy]' --break-system-packages
litellm --model openai/qwen \
  --api_base http://localhost:8080/v1 \
  --api_key dummy --port 4000

export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://localhost:4000
export ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN=dummy
export ANTHROPIC_MODEL=qwen
export ANTHROPIC_SMALL_FAST_MODEL=qwen
  • Alternative: claude-code-router — purpose-built proxy for Claude Code with per-task model routing

Tool-call expectations

  • OpenCode: best of the bunch for local — provider-aware, handles smaller-model quirks
  • Claude Code: works but rough — Claude Code expects frontier-model quality tool calls; expect malformed JSON occasionally
  • All tools: bump -c to 64k+ for usable agentic work (tools eat context fast)
  • If tool calls fail repeatedly → add --chat-template chatml to llama-server

6. Verify performance

llama-bench -m ~/models/Qwen3.6-27B-Q4_K_M.gguf -ngl 99 -fa 1
  • Expected on M3 Max for 27B Q4_K_M:
    • Prompt eval: ~200–400 tok/s
    • Generation: ~18–22 tok/s
  • If gen <10 tok/s → swapping. Close Chrome/Docker, check sudo memory_pressure

Optimization Knobs (matter a lot)

  • Quant level: 4-bit is the sweet spot. Below 4-bit = noticeable quality loss
  • Context length: KV cache scales linearly. Drop to 8k–16k unless you need long context
  • Flash attention: always enable on M-series (--flash-attn on)
  • KV cache quantization: q8_0 halves memory with negligible quality hit
  • Speculative decoding: pair big model with tiny draft model → 1.5–2x speedup
    • Example: 27B target + 1.5B draft, both same family
    • Best gains on predictable text (code, structured output)
  • Memory pressure: keep ~6GB free for macOS or you'll swap and tank tok/s
  • Unified memory caveat: Chrome/Docker/etc fight for the same pool. Close before long sessions

Speculative Decoding Example

llama-server \
  -m ~/models/Qwen3.6-27B-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  -md ~/models/Qwen3-1.5B-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  -ngl 99 -ngld 99 \
  --draft-max 16 --draft-min 4 \
  --flash-attn on -c 8192
  • Draft model generates N tokens, big model verifies in one pass
  • -md = draft model path, -ngld = draft model GPU layers

Models That Won't Fit on 36GB

These are the current frontier open models — all need data-center GPUs:

  • Kimi K2.6 (Moonshot) — 1T total / 32B active MoE
    • Smallest viable quant: 350GB (2-bit dynamic GGUF)
    • Needs 8x H100 for production
  • DeepSeek-V4-Pro — 1.6T total / 49B active MoE
    • 1M-token context with hybrid CSA/HCA attention
    • Even V4-Flash (284B/13B active) needs ~140GB at 4-bit
  • GLM-5.1 (zai-org) — 754B total / 40B active MoE
    • Smallest quant (Unsloth dynamic 1-bit): 200GB
    • Strong on SWE-Bench Pro and Terminal-Bench 2.0

warning: MoE saves compute, not memory. All experts must stay resident. Active param count (the smaller number) only tells you inference cost, not RAM requirement.

For these models: use APIs (OpenRouter, DeepInfra, provider direct) instead of local hosting.

Other Models That Fit on 36GB

  • Gemma 3 27B (~16GB at 4-bit) — strong general reasoning, multimodal
  • Qwen2.5-Coder 32B (~18GB at 4-bit) — previous default, still solid
  • Llama 3.3 70B at IQ2_XXS (~22GB) — pushes limits, slower, quality dips noticeably
  • Qwen3 14B / Gemma 3 12B at 4-bit — fast, leaves headroom for big context

Common Gotchas

  • Forgot -ngl 99 → runs on CPU, 10x slower
  • Context too large → OOM crash. Watch sudo memory_pressure while running
  • Wrong chat template → garbage output. Pass --chat-template chatml|llama3|gemma if auto-detect fails
  • Gated model 401 → accept license in browser first, even with valid token
  • Partial GGUF download → cryptic errors. Verify ls -lh matches HF size
  • Flag drift: llama.cpp renames flags often. Recent breakage:
    • --flash-attn → now requires value: --flash-attn on|off|auto
    • Run llama-server -h | grep <flag> if a flag errors

Quick Alias

Add to ~/.zshrc:

alias llm-serve='llama-server -m ~/models/Qwen3.6-27B-Q4_K_M.gguf -ngl 99 -c 16384 --flash-attn on --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0 --port 8080'

Alternative Runtimes

  • MLX / mlx-lm — Apple's native framework, ~10–30% faster on Apple Silicon
    • Separate runtime, separate model format (MLX folder, not GGUF — no interop with llama.cpp)
    • Use when raw throughput matters more than ecosystem/quant variety
    • Install: pip install mlx-lm --break-system-packages
    • Download: hf download unsloth/Qwen3.6-27B-UD-MLX-4bit --local-dir ~/models/qwen3.6-mlx
    • Run: mlx_lm.server --model ~/models/qwen3.6-mlx --port 8080
    • Tradeoffs: smaller model selection, fewer quant variants, no spec decoding yet
  • Ollama — wraps llama.cpp, easier ergonomics, model registry
    • Use as always-on daemon: brew install ollama && ollama serve
    • Endpoint at http://localhost:11434/v1
  • LM Studio — GUI for browsing/comparing quants
    • Bundles both MLX and llama.cpp runtimes (pick per model)

Resources

  • llama.cpp repo
  • hf CLI docs
  • bartowski's GGUF quants — go-to source for community GGUF quants
  • unsloth — both GGUF and MLX, often with dynamic quants
  • mlx-community — MLX-formatted models
  • LiteLLM proxy docs

Overview

Understanding how to optimize ML/AI training at the GPU kernel level through custom CUDA programming, quantization techniques, and hardware-specific optimizations. This knowledge is critical for building high-performance ML infrastructure and understanding the lowest levels of neural network training optimization.

Inspiration: Cursor's blog post about achieving 3.5x speedup in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layer performance through custom MXFP8 kernels on Blackwell GPUs, demonstrating that custom kernel development can unlock massive performance gains beyond what standard libraries provide.

Motivation

  • Understand how ML/AI infrastructure works at the GPU kernel level, not just high-level frameworks
  • Learn custom kernel development for performance optimization (moving beyond PyTorch/TensorFlow abstractions)
  • Comprehend quantization techniques (MXFP8, FP8, BF16) for efficient training at scale
  • Understand modern GPU architectures (Hopper, Blackwell) and their implications for ML workloads
  • Gain ability to identify and fix performance bottlenecks in ML training pipelines
  • Real-world impact: Cursor achieved 1.5x end-to-end training improvements on Blackwell and 2x gains vs Hopper

Key Concepts

1. GPU Architecture Fundamentals

Hardware Components:

  • Tensor cores: Specialized hardware for matrix multiplication operations
  • Shared memory: Fast on-chip memory shared within a threadblock
  • Register hierarchies: L1/L2 cache, registers, and memory bandwidth considerations
  • Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs): Basic execution units on GPU

Architecture Evolution:

  • Hopper architecture: Register-based accumulation for tensor operations
  • Blackwell architecture: Introduces Tensor Memory (TMEM) - new on-chip storage
    • TMEM requires asynchronous data movement to registers
    • Creates pipeline bubbles where dequantization can take 1.76x the time of matrix multiplication
    • Requires different optimization strategies than Hopper

Key Challenge: "Quantization time can truly kill the performance gain" - up to 76% of theoretical speedup can be lost to poorly optimized quantization

2. CUDA Programming & Kernel Optimization

Low-Level Programming:

  • PTX instructions: Assembly-level GPU programming
  • tcgen05.mma instruction: Hardware-managed block scaling for efficient quantization
  • Warp specialization: Assigning specialized warpgroups to different pipeline stages
  • Memory synchronization: Managing data flow between TMEM, registers, and global memory

Optimization Patterns:

  • 2-CTA matrix multiplication mode: 15-20% speedups through collaborative SM execution
  • Persistent grid pattern: Scheduling one threadblock per SM for continuous operation
  • Expert-wise supergrouping: L2 cache optimization strategies for grouped matrix operations
  • Pipeline design: Overlapping computation and memory transfer to hide latency

3. Low-Precision Training & Quantization

MXFP8 Format (Microscaled Floating-Point):

  • Uses FP8E4M3 elements (8-bit floating point: 1 sign, 4 exponent, 3 mantissa bits)
  • 32-block scaling: Scale factors applied per 32-element blocks
  • Maintains training quality comparable to BF16 (nearly indistinguishable loss curves)
  • Reduces memory bandwidth requirements significantly

Precision Formats Comparison:

  • BF16 (Brain Float 16): Standard high-precision training format
  • FP8: 8-bit floating point (E4M3 or E5M2 variants)
  • MXFP8: Block-scaled FP8 with per-block scale factors
  • INT8: Integer quantization (typically for inference)

Trade-offs:

  • Precision vs Memory Bandwidth: Lower precision = less data movement
  • Precision vs Training Quality: Must maintain convergence properties
  • Quantization Overhead: Time spent quantizing/dequantizing must be less than bandwidth savings

Quantization Optimization Example:

  • Cursor achieved 6.2+ TB/s bandwidth utilization (vs 4.5 TB/s from TransformerEngine/TorchAO)
  • Key: Producing scale factors in exact layout expected by tensor core instructions
  • Eliminates costly reshape operations that can dominate runtime

4. Matrix Multiplication Optimization for MoE

Grouped Matrix Multiplication Variants:

  • Fprop (Forward propagation): Input × Weights
  • Dgrad (Data gradient): Error × Weights^T
  • Wgrad (Weight gradient): Input^T × Error

Block-Scaling Concepts:

  • Per-block vs per-tensor scaling strategies
  • Hardware-managed scaling with tensor cores
  • Impact on accumulation precision

Performance Bottlenecks:

  • Quantization overhead can dominate if not optimized
  • Memory bandwidth saturation limits
  • Pipeline bubbles from synchronization
  • Cache coherency in grouped operations

Metrics to Track:

  • Memory bandwidth utilization: TB/s achieved vs theoretical maximum
  • Occupancy: Percentage of GPU resources actively used
  • Pipeline efficiency: Ratio of compute time to synchronization/transfer time
  • Quantization overhead: Time spent in quantize/dequantize operations

  • GPU profiling tools (NVIDIA Nsight, nvprof)
  • Understanding SM utilization patterns
  • Identifying memory-bound vs compute-bound operations
  • Bottleneck analysis (where is time actually spent?)

In summary, Kafka streams provide a way to process and analyze data in motion, and topics serve as the channels through which the data is ingested, processed, and distributed. The combination of topics and streams allows for a powerful and flexible data processing architecture in Kafka.

Kafka broker

  • Node
  • Responsible for persistence
  • Contains leader topics and replica topics

Kafka topic

  • Logical channel in a Kafka broker
  • Has multiple partitions
  • Leader will copy to replica

Kafka topic partition

  • Partition of a topic
  • Producers can emit to the topic partition
  • Consumers can consume from the topic partition
  • (For more info: look into ad service system)

Kafka streams

  • Consumes topic and streams in real time

Dead Letter Queue

  • After a timeout of no acknowledge from consumer, send event to DLQ

Consumer Groups

  • Group of Consumers
  • Single consumer group pattern - distribute load (each partition is assigned a consumer from the cg)
  • Multi consumer group pattern - broadcast (each consumer group will receive the same message)

Consumers

  • Consumer service (could be fargate, etc)
  • Each partition will be assigned a consumer
  • Each consumer can take on multiple partitions

Amazon Managed Streaming (AWS MSK)

  • Managed Streaming for Kafka service
  • Auto scaling storage capacity
  • Compute capacity automatically scales up (not horizontal)
  • Manual scaling number of brokers

Avro

  • Messages commonly use Avro schema

Offsets

  • Must have, way of keeping track where the consumer's progress is in a partition
  • Typical pattern is storing offset state for all consumers in another topic (a __consumer_offsets)

Apache Kafka

atomic = all or nothing distributed transactions

  • transaction - an operation
  • distributed - one operation made up of many operations on multiple decoupled systems transactional = atomic = all or nothing

Distributed transactions (atomic)

a way to determine should a transaction commit across all participants (ensuring all participants agree and are on the same page)

  • 2-phase commit
    • 2 steps
      • prepare / vote
      • commit
    • all databases are atomic and when 1 database aborts, the entire transaction to all databases aborts
    • Strong consistency (read after write)
    • Helps have ACID in distributed databases
    • https://medium.com/geekculture/distributed-transactions-two-phase-commit-c82752d69324
    • Acts as a single ACID commit
    • problem: if coordinator dies before telling everyone, then all participants are idle
  • 3-phase commit
    • 3 steps
      • prepare / vote
      • pre-commit
      • commit
    • solves problem of 2-phase commit, middle step of pre-commit, will broadcast to the participants on the decision
      • if participant got pre-commit message, it will proceed with a commit as it knows it is safe
      • if participant does not, it aborts
  • SAGA
    • Eventual consistency
    • Multiple commits sequentially (and rolling back each step upon failure)
    • Simulates distributed transactions by having the programming model simulate consistency
    • Need a state field in the db usually (to say it’s done)

Atomic

Domain Events

Create (aka Raise) and Consume (aka Publish) events https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AHzWJ_SMqLo

Usage flow

  • EntityFramework (EF) will track changes to the entity objects
  • Each entity object will have a list of domain events for the given entity
  • When performing ******Outbox Pattern the entities changes tracked are fetched (via ChangeTracker) and obtain all domain events
  • Create outbox message for each domain event
  • Save all outbox message
  • EF generates sql command for all changes (original and new outbox messages changes) to ensure atomicity
  • Commits transaction

Outbox Pattern

Intercept db action and modify db context to include another change in the same transaction Then consume those intercepted atomic entries separately https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XALvnX7MPeo https://chatgpt.com/share/67da2996-db10-8001-a544-b71f1a56e105

public async Task PlaceNewOrder()
{
    var order = new Order("12345");
    
    // 1) This raises a domain event inside the AggregateRoot
    order.PlaceOrder(); 

	// 2) Entity is now tracked by ChangeTracker
    _dbContext.Orders.Add(order); 

	// 3) The interceptor will process this!
    await _dbContext.SaveChangesAsync(); 
}


// 1) domain events


public class Order : AggregateRoot
{
    public string OrderNumber { get; private set; }

    public void PlaceOrder()
    {
        // Raise a domain event when an order is placed
        RaiseDomainEvent(new OrderPlacedEvent(this.Id));
    }
}

public class AggregateRoot : Entity
{
	// multiple domain events per object
	private List<DomainEvents> _domainEvents == new();

	// add
	public RaiseDomainEvent(DomainEvent domainEvent);

	// get
	public GetDomainEvents();
	
	// clear
	public ClearDomainEvents();
}


// 2) interceptor


public class DomainEventsInterceptor : SaveChangesInterceptor
{
    public override async ValueTask<int> SavedChangesAsync(
        SaveChangesCompletedEventData eventData, 
        int result, 
        CancellationToken cancellationToken = default)
    {
        var context = eventData.Context;
        if (context == null) return result;

        // Step 1: Get all domain events from AggregateRoots
        var domainEvents = context.ChangeTracker.Entries<AggregateRoot>()
            .SelectMany(e => e.Entity.GetDomainEvents())
            .ToList();

        if (domainEvents.Any())
        {
            // Step 2: Convert domain events into Outbox Messages
            var outboxMessages = domainEvents.Select(e => new OutboxMessage(e)).ToList();

            // Step 3: Persist outbox messages
            await context.Set<OutboxMessage>().AddRangeAsync(outboxMessages, cancellationToken);

            // Step 4: Call base method to persist outbox messages (and the original db changes)
            await base.SavedChangesAsync(eventData, result, cancellationToken);

            // Step 5: Clear domain events from AggregateRoot
            foreach (var entity in context.ChangeTracker.Entries<AggregateRoot>())
            {
                entity.Entity.ClearDomainEvents();
            }
        }

        return result;
    }
}

Policy-based Authorization

Background

In ASP.NET Core, policy-based authorization is a flexible way to enforce access control. It involves requirements, handlers, and policies.

under the hood, role-based authorization and claims-based authorization use a requirement and a preconfigured policy

Requirement

resembles an authorization requirement the logic is implemented by a handler(s) the requirement is consumed in a policy

public class MinimumAgeRequirement : IAuthorizationRequirement
{
    public int MinimumAge { get; }
    public MinimumAgeRequirement(int minimumAge) => MinimumAge = minimumAge;
}

Handler

responsible for evaluation logic for requirement(s) the handler is registered in DI

public class MinimumAgeHandler : AuthorizationHandler<MinimumAgeRequirement>
{
    protected override Task HandleRequirementAsync(
        AuthorizationHandlerContext context,
        MinimumAgeRequirement requirement)
    {
        if (context.User.HasClaim(c => c.Type == "Age"))
        {
            int age = int.Parse(context.User.FindFirst(c => c.Type == "Age").Value);
            if (age >= requirement.MinimumAge)
            {
                context.Succeed(requirement);
            }
        }
        return Task.CompletedTask;
    }
}

Policy (Registration)

builder.Services.AddAuthorization(options =>
{
    options.AddPolicy("AdultOnly", policy =>
        policy.Requirements.Add(new MinimumAgeRequirement(18)));
});

builder.Services.AddSingleton<IAuthorizationHandler, MinimumAgeHandler>();

Register a handler

Usage

[Authorize(Policy = "AdultOnly")]
public IActionResult RestrictedAccess()
{
    return Ok("You have access!");
}

var authResult = await _authorizationService.AuthorizeAsync(User, null, "AdultOnly");
if (authResult.Succeeded)
{
    // Grant access
}

Use IAuthorizationService, [Authorize(Policy = "Something")], or RequireAuthorization("Something") for authorization.

Mapping

different types are handler -> requirement mapping

One-to-one Authorization

  • [one handler for one requirement](A requirement can have multiple handlers. A handler may inherit AuthorizationHandler, where TRequirement is the requirement to be handled. Alternatively, a handler may implement IAuthorizationHandler directly to handle more than one type of requirement.)

One-to-many Authorization ("AND" Authorization)

  • one handler for multiple requirements
  • policy has multiple requirements
  • handler has logic to handle multiple requirements

Many-to-one Authorization (for "OR" Authorization (chain))

  • many handlers per requirement
  • policy has 1 requirement, but many handlers as options to fulfill the requirement
  • uses public class [Badge/TempBadge]EntryHandler : AuthorizationHandler<BuildingEntryRequirement>

Basics

Terms

  • Type - blueprint defines structure (value type and reference type)
    • Class - reference type
    • (Member - general term refers to elements in a class (such as: fields, methods, etc))
    • Field - variable in a class (assigned a type)
    • Property - mechanism to read/write/compute on private field (include accessor methods) (getters/setters)
    • Attribute - metadata applied to classes, methods, properties (not data storage, but metadata)

Type

  • Value Type (primitive)
    • Kinda like primitives

    • null: not allowed (?)
    • Examples: int, float, bool, char, struct, enum
  • Reference Type (class)
    • Memory: allocated on heap
    • Garbage Collection: managed
    • Upon assignment to another variable: shared memory
    • null: allowed
    • Examples: class, interface, delegate, array, string
  • Type Members
    • Fields: Variables that hold data
    • Properties: Accessors for fields
    • Methods: Functions that perform operations
    • Events: Notifications that something has occurred
    • Constructors: Methods called when an instance is created
    • Destructors: Methods called when an instance is destroyed

Data Structures

public - Accessible from any other code in the same assembly or referencing assembly private - Accessible only within the same class or struct protected - Accessible within the same class and derived classes internal - Accessible within the same assembly static - Belongs to the type itself, not to a specific object instance

public class Result<T>
{
    public T Value { get; }
    public Error Error { get; }

    private Result(T value)
    {
        Value = value;
        IsSuccess = true;
    }

    private Result(Error error)
    {
        Error = error;
        IsSuccess = false;
    }

	// implicit operators
    public static implicit operator Result<T>(T value) 
    => new Result<T>(value);
    
    public static implicit operator Result<T>(Error error) 
    => new Result<T>(error);

  • PascalCase for types, namespaces, and all public members

Cache storages are used to reduce read and writes to disk by storing memory in RAM

Use cases:

  • low latency
  • Improve disk (or DB) performance

Suitable for data that is:

  • Frequently accessed
  • Short lived
  • (Network cache) Needs to be shared throughout multiple distributed instances

Redis

A redis cache cluster is an in memory cache cluster that the application can make network calls to access. It is in memory since the data is stored in RAM on the cluster.

Off Heap Memory

Off heap cache is memory stored in RAM to be used as a cache directly on the application instance.

Pros:

  • Faster
  • More secure and private
  • Easier to maintain Cons:
  • Can't be used from multiple distributed instances without distributed locks

Intro

  • wtfs per minute

  • princples patterns and practices

Chapter 1: Clean code

  • we will always have code
  • specifying requirements is programming
  • the specification is code
  • sure there will be abstractions, but we will always need code
  • Bad code
    • wading - slowed down by bad code
    • ambiguity of purpose
    • muddled intent
    • room for speculation
  • Clean code
    • focused
    • crisp on writers intent
    • easy for other ppl to enhance it
    • no duplication
    • method - says what it does
      • impl - says how it is done
        • wrap particular implementation in a more abstract method or class
  • total cost of owning a mess
    • asymptotically lowers productivity
    • each change requires untangling and understanding
  • a broken window in an apt causes other ppl to not care and make a mess
  • doing 1 thing
    • object or a method should just focus on 1 thing
  • Ron Jeffries
    • no duplication
    • one thing
    • expressiveness
    • tiny abstractions
  • we read old code 10x more than writing during writing. so we want old code to be easy to read -> easy to read = easy to write

Chapter 2: Meaningful Names

  • intention-revealing names
  • never distinguish 2 things by using non-distinguishing name
    • ex: doing account vs theAccount (bc cant have duplicates in scope)
    • if there's a different object or function, explicitly describe the intention / difference
  • length of name can correspond to size of scope
    • one letter name is OK if it's a tiny scope
  • make things searchable
    • ex: using a const instead of a magic number
  • avoid prefix, use class: using prefix is ok when adding context of a larger structure BUT using class is better
    • prefix ex: addressState, addressFirstName, etc
    • class ex: Address.state
  • add details from page 29
    • split large functions with lots of repeat variable usage -> to a class with small functions

Chapter 3: Functions

  • SMALL SMALL SMALL
  • DO JUST ONE THING
    • how to classify as just 1 thing -> 1 layer of abstraction
    • to "TO" test -> "TO {function name} we do x, y, z"
    • another way to tell -> if you can extract small function and it's not just a re-statement
    • another way to tell -> if you divide into sections
  • combine with meaningful and intention-revealing names
  • split large functions -> a class (? when to split to class vs smaller methods)
  • blocks within if, else, while should be 1 line long (functional call)
  • results in documentation in the form of being descriptive
  • max indent level - 1 or 2 arguments
  • max arguments - 3 maxxx
    • 0 or 1 or 2
    • 0 - ideal
      • make it part of the class, use class variables
    • 1 - ok for taking in input
    • 2 - ok for related to single component (ex: an xy point)
    • more arguments, more complicated tests, more cognitive load, probably doing more than 1 thing
    • if you need more than 1, mostly use an object
  • don't use arguments for outputs
  • don't use arguments for flags - means function is doing more than 1 thing naming
  • name should describe intent (and intent of arguments)
    • ex: assertExpectedEqualsActual(expected, equals)
  • consistent logic
  • DRY
  • no side effects
  • command and query separation - should either do something or answer, not both
    • bad example: public boolean set(String attribute, String value) returns true when successful is confusing
      • if(set("username", "unclebob)) is confusing. is it true if previously set, successfully set? etc is set adjective or verb error handling
  • use exceptions instead of returning error code
  • error handling IS 1 thing
    • have 1 dedicated method for try catching logic
    • and extract try and catch logic to another function dependency magnet
  • ex: error code class that is used everywhere. change to this requires re-compile of tons of classes
  • instead, use something that is derivatives (oops), like exception classes

Chapter 4: Comments

  • comments at best are evil
  • comments compensate for our failure to express in code

Chapter 5: Formatting

  • use a consistent format file
  • newspaper method - top to bottom, order of detail (high level to lower level details)
  • use lines to separate concepts
  • vertical density - more for close relation
  • vertical distance - separate concepts/relations structure
  • closely related concepts should be in the same file variables
  • declaration should be vertically close as possible to their usage
  • instance variables used by many methods - put at the top functions
  • dependent functions should be vertically close. caller should be above callee.
  • dependencies flows downwards
  • for constants input into a function, makes more sense to have it as the input where it makes it easy to read and quickly understand what that method will do instead of hiding it in a lower level method

notes.html:
related to N different systems doing their operations all or nothing (online order - shipping, stock count, payment) measure of how in sync 2+ storage systems are in terms of writing then reading

Types (levels of consistency)

Strong consistency (read after write)

  • Updates can be read instantly after a write (higher latency)
  • Example: transactions to withdraw from bank A and save to bank B (either all are complete, or non complete), shouldn’t be a case where half is complete when reading.
  • Using locks to synchronize under the hood
  • using Consensus (internally to the distributed storage system) to implement

Eventual consistency

  • Updates can be read after x time after updates (lower latency, but risk of stale data)
  • A read may not read at a valid state as it is eventually consistent but maybe not at the time of read
  • Consistency refers to reading a valid state at any time all the time

When there are multiple storage systems in a system, synchronization has to be done somehow to align them

notes.html:
Hashing allows us to map a key to a number that represents a node

In large scale systems, one cluster (cache cluster, server cluster, db cluster) is not enough

Hashing can be used to determine which node should be used for the given request

Simple Hashing

  • HashFunction(key) % N
  • N is number of nodes
  • HashFunction looks to distribute evenly
  • Issue: what if N changes, all keys are now corrupt as the same node won't be used

Consistent Hashing

  • Aimed to have consistent node assignment even has N changes
  • Hash the key and server name
  • Range of x0 to xN (Hash Space)
  • Implementation
    • Make 0->N in a ring
    • HashFunction(server name/ip)
    • HashFunction(key)
    • Retrieve
      • Find Hash of key and go clockwise until a server found
    • If N changes, only one range of keys gets lost
    • Issue: distribution of objects may be uneven
      • Solution: Virtual Nodes, spread apart a single node on the ring as virtual nodes
      • Now nodes won't be starved of traffic
      • Takes metadata for maintaining virtual nodes
  • Real life usages
    • DynamoDB and Cassandra - Data Partitioning
      • Minimizes data movement during rebalances
    • Content Delivery Networks - Distribute web content
    • Load Balancer - Distribute persistent connections evenly

notes.html:
In distributed systems, often times a central coordination service is needed between nodes.

Apache ZooKeeper

Apache ZooKeeper is an example of a coordination service that can be used to coordinate nodes.

Use Case

NoSQL with Strong Consistency for Unique Id Generation

  • This example stems from the URL Shortener system design, where a unique id needs to be created but ensured it's not in use
    • in SQL we are ACID compliant and can use putIfAbsent for Strong consistency (read after write)
    • in NoSQL, we are running on Eventual consistency due to the nature of how it scales horizontally
    • Checking if it exists each new post / put request is expensive and not viable
  • We want to use NoSQL for the scalability, but can not have eventual consistency as it is a risk of having collision, this is how we can achieve NoSQL with Strong Consistency when generating ids:
    1. A number from a counter can be used to create random unique ids (using encoding or hashing) and ensure it has not been used before (since it increments)
    2. Lets say you have an application with many instances / nodes and is regionally distributed and we need to keep track of a counter 1 - 100,000,000 between all instances and be synchronized
    3. We can use ZooKeeper to coordinate instance 1 counts: 0 - 10,000,000 instance 2 counts: 10,000,001 - 20,000,000 ... and when an instance counter reaches the limit, the coordination service will tell the instance the next range to use and if an instance goes down, that range will simply be unused or paused

Strategy Pattern

  • Avoid a ton if statements
  • Polymorphism
  • Implementation: use Map of different child classes
  • Example: reverse polish notation, valid parentheses

Decorator Pattern

  • Extend object without changing original implementation
  • Open Close Principle
  • Sort of like a wrapper
    • Implement an interface
    • Pass in the original instance of impl of interface
    • Call the original instance method but do extra stuff around

Observer Pattern

  • Notify subscribers

Singleton Pattern

  • Single object everywhere
  • Example
    • Database access (repo)
    • Don't want a new instance every request
  • Implementation

    • static variable of instance of self
    • getInstance() returns that instance
    • not thread safe, use synchronize on the static variable

Facade Pattern

  • Wrapper to hide complexity
  • Wrapper also creates one place to change if underlying framework changes

notes.html:
A lock to protect a resource accessed by distributed machines

Approaches

Single lock service ❌

  • Single point of failure

Lock DB with async replication ❌

  • Eventual consistency leading to multiple clients with lock at the same time

Lock DB with sync replication ❌

  • Not fault tolerant
  • If leader needs to replicate to all followers, if 1 follower is down, can't proceed

Lock DB with Quorum Consensus using Fencing Token ❌

  • A little more fault tolerant but not linearizable (not in order)
  • Might update 1 replicate, and other replicate is down (need Two Phase Commit (2pc) to fix that)
  • Quorum Consensus helps with fault tolerance but is not linearizable
  • Quorum Consensus is not linearizable since
  • What if some client finds a max Fencing Token (from > n/2 replicas) and needs to update, but the client fails to update because it went down
    • Then another client can read from > n/2 outdated replicas

Lock DB with Distributed Consensus using Fencing Token ✅

  • Fault tolerant and linearizable
  • Distributed Consensus majority must accept (Two Phase Commit (2pc))
  • Example: RAFT
  • If leader fails, a up to date follower will be elected to leader (max Fencing Key)
  • Use this to guarantee who has the Lock with:
    • Fault Tolerance
    • Fencing Key used if somehow two clients have the Lock
      • two clients can get the Lock accidentally if a client has some process pause (ex: Garbage Collector) and hits TTL of Lock service and Lock is released
      • In this case the Fencing Key can be used to break the tie

notes.html:
A workflow (e.g. order checkout) is done in a durable fashion (fulfills even if servers go down)

essentially a durable message queue / job orchestrator with cached results (so you can tie multiple steps together and can replay steps upon workflow retry)

opensource framework: temporal

workflow: a function be to ran durably activity: a workflow step with external dependency node: server that runs the workflow and activities

checkpoint: last tracked successful state (note: it's not actually restarting from checkpoint, rather it restarts from scratch but uses cached activity results instead of re-running the already done activity)

features

  • at-least-once execution
    • the workflow will restart if incomplete until the entire workflow is completed
  • resuming
    • resume from checkpoint
    • this is important for
      • non-deterministic activity
        • (example: claude code workflow, call LLM activity, imagine node crashes and restarts session and new LLM responses were in the chat - bad experience)
      • async / long wait activity (human input)
  • abstraction
    • abstract away the distributed systems complexities of durability for any function

limitation

  • lacking at-most-once (exactly once) execution
    • more complex
    • restarting from checkpoint means the activity could have ran but node crashed before tracking activity finished, thus activity re-runs
    • compensate by making activities idempotent
  • it is not for Atomic / transactional
    • you can pair durable execution with SAGA or outbox to handle distributed transaction (if credit card step passes, but shipping fails ?)

retrying workflows

when: upon failure detection

  • timeout, heart beat, etc what:
  • retries from start but "skip" to last tracked step how:
  • log when an activity starts
  • log when an activity ends
  • cache the result of the activity that ran
  • so retry actually just replays

durable execution vs durable message queue

job orchestrator like a processing/handling a message from a Message Queue and running the job, would re-run the entire job from the start upon a node failure

whereas, durable executor is more granular - it would resume from last tracked successful state

so sub steps (activities) like

  • human approval or input
    • durable execution can simply replay from cache (instead of redoing or re-waiting)
  • non-deterministic call like LLM
    • durable execution can simply replay from cache (instead of retry leading to another value)

DynamoDB is a NoSQL AWS managed serverless database that scales.

Global Tables

  • Eventual consistency
  • Global tables replicate your DynamoDB tables automatically across your choice of AWS Regions
  • Replication lag is under 1 second
  • To help ensure eventual consistency, DynamoDB global tables use a last-writer-wins reconciliation between concurrent updates, in which DynamoDB makes a best effort to determine the last writer. Transactions

token embeddings = 1 vector to represent a token text embeddings = 1 vector to represents text (sentence(s)) process to get text embeddings: (token embeddings -> transformer -> contextual embeddings -> pooling -> text embedding)

GPT LLM model = decoder = attention to everything before Embedding model = encoder = attention to everything before AND after input, understand, output = encoder-decoder (like translation)

training an embedding model:

  • pretraining on transformer (learn the language)
    • masked token prediction (common for encoder models) -> encoder-based embeddings
    • or next-token predicition (common for decoder models) -> decoder-based embeddings
    • or encoder-decoder model
    • or another large-scale language objective
  • contrastive embedding training (learn similarities)
    • train on pairs or groups
    • query, positive, negative

during LLM (decoder architecture) pretraining:

  • Also trains an embeddings model implicitly (but not specialized for similarity)
  • Every Transformer layer produces hidden vectors for the tokens
    • Those vectors contain information about the whole preceding context

  • Yes, many dedicated embedding models are trained with contrastive learning.

    • Similar text pairs are pulled closer in vector space.
    • Unrelated text pairs are pushed farther apart.
    • Example:
      • “How do I reset my password?”
      • “Password reset instructions”
      • These should get nearby vectors.

  • Embedding models are usually separate from GPT-style LLMs.

    • GPT model:
      • Main goal: predict the next token.
      • Usually decoder-only.
      • Output: text tokens.
    • Embedding model:
      • Main goal: produce a useful vector for similarity/search.
      • Often encoder-only, though other architectures can work.
      • Output: one vector for the input text.

  • But embedding models can still benefit from LLM-style pretraining.

    • Common process:
      1. Pretrain a Transformer on lots of text.
      2. Then train or fine-tune it with a contrastive embedding objective.
    • So it can first learn language generally, then learn:
      • which sentences mean similar things,
      • which queries match which documents,
      • how to organize meaning in vector space.

  • It does not have to be trained from a GPT model specifically.

    • GPT is decoder-only.
    • Many embedding models start from encoder models, such as BERT-like architectures.
    • Some modern systems also use decoder-only LLMs and adapt their hidden states into embeddings.
    • The important part is the final embedding-specific training objective, not whether it started as GPT.

Encoder vs decoder

  • Encoder
    • Reads the input text.
    • Produces contextual vectors.
    • Usually can look at tokens on both sides of each token.
    • Good for:
      • embeddings,
      • classification,
      • search,
      • understanding text.
text → encoder → vectors
  • Decoder
    • Generates tokens one at a time.
    • Looks at previous tokens and predicts the next one.
    • Good for:
      • writing,
      • answering questions,
      • generating code.
previous tokens → decoder → next token
  • Encoder–decoder
    • The encoder reads and understands the input.
    • The decoder generates a new output based on the encoder’s representations.
    • Common for:
      • translation,
      • summarization,
      • text-to-text tasks.
English sentence
      ↓
   encoder
      ↓
internal representations
      ↓
   decoder
      ↓
French sentence

Example:

Encoder reads:
"Translate 'hello' to French"

Decoder generates:
"bonjour"

Token embeddings vs text embeddings

  • Token embedding
    • Represents one token.
    • A token may be:
      • a whole word,
      • part of a word,
      • punctuation,
      • a few characters.
    • Example:
"unbelievable"

might become:
["un", "believ", "able"]

Each token gets its own starting vector.

  • Text embedding
    • Represents the meaning of the entire input.
    • It may summarize:
      • one sentence,
      • multiple sentences,
      • a paragraph,
      • a document chunk.
"The dog is running through the park."
        ↓
one text embedding vector

How they are related

  • Yes, they are related parts of the same processing pipeline.
Text
 ↓
Tokenizer
 ↓
Token IDs
 ↓
Token embedding lookup
 ↓
One starting vector per token
 ↓
Transformer layers
 ↓
One contextual vector per token
 ↓
Pooling / projection
 ↓
One text embedding
  • Step by step:
    • The tokenizer converts text into token IDs.
    • The token embedding table converts each token ID into a starting vector.
    • The Transformer modifies those vectors using context.
    • The final token vectors now contain contextual meaning.
    • The model combines those token vectors into one text embedding.

Example:

"The bank approved my loan"

Initial token vectors:

"The"  → vector
"bank" → vector
"approved" → vector
"my" → vector
"loan" → vector

After the Transformer, the vector for “bank” understands that it means a financial institution.

Then the model combines all the contextual token vectors into one vector representing the full sentence.

The simplest distinction

  • Token embedding: starting vector for one token.
  • Contextual token representation: that token’s vector after Transformer processing.
  • Text embedding: one combined vector representing the whole input.
  • GPT output: probabilities over possible next tokens.

So the full relationship is:

token embeddings are inputs to the Transformer

contextual token vectors are outputs of Transformer layers

text embeddings ar

e created by combining those contextual token vectors

Generic Method Argument Types

Methods in C# can be generic, which means they can work with different types without the need to write separate methods for each type.

The types specified in the angle brackets <> are placeholders that get replaced with actual types when the method is called.

public class GenericExample
{
    public T FindMax<T>(T first, T second) 
    where T : IComparable<T>
    {
        return first.CompareTo(second) > 0 ? first : second;
    }
}

class Program
{
    static void Main(string[] args)
    {
        GenericExample example = new GenericExample();

        // Using with integers
        int maxInt = example.FindMax(10, 20);
        // Output: Max integer: 20
        Console.WriteLine($"Max integer: {maxInt}"); 

        // Using with doubles
        double maxDouble = example.FindMax(3.14, 2.71);
        // Output: Max double: 3.14
        Console.WriteLine($"Max double: {maxDouble}"); 

        // Using with strings
        string maxString = example.FindMax("apple", "banana");
        // Output: Max string: banana
        Console.WriteLine($"Max string: {maxString}"); 
    }
}

Background

Language: Java

Usages:

  • Microservices
  • Event-Driven Architecture
  • Dependency Injection

Description

  • A dependency injection framework for Java that has many web and backend plugins

Types

Reactive

  • Spring WebFlux (Reactive)
  • Asynchronous threads, non-blocking, event loop
  • Event-Driven Architecture
  • Netty
  • Request gets assigned to thread
  • Functional Programming / Reactive Programming
  • Complex to code, but more thread efficient
  • HTTP Client: WebClient

Servlet

  • Spring MVC
  • Synchronous threads (blocking)
  • Thread per request
  • Imperative Programming
  • Simpler to code, but less efficient
  • HTTP Client: RestTemplate (deprecated)

Examples

  • Restaurant
    • Reactive:
      1. server takes queue of orders (events)
      2. cook "subscribes" to queue of meals to prepare
      3. cook "publishes" to waiters queue to serve once meal is done
      • each threads are optimally used
    • Servlet:
      1. server takes order
      2. cook prepares (30min)
      3. serve food
      4. repeat
      • each order is a new thread

SpringBoot

SpringBoot is a bootstrap for Spring

Spring Security

OAuth implementation built in to Spring

Classes

  • Principal: Authentication Object (Bearer Token)
  • UserDetails: User Object
  • Geogram Example Implementation

Thread Safety

https://stackoverflow.com/questions/43314831/spring-boot-class-behaviour

  • When using @Bean @Autowired or any method of creating a singleton class, one instance will be created and shared for the entire application (unless @Scope is defined)
  • Each request to the application is a on its own thread
  • Static variables by nature are shared amongst all instances, so it is shared amongst all threads
  • Class-level variables will be shared amongst all threads for a singleton, since it's one shared instance of the class used for all requests
  • For data that should not be shared, create a new instance of that non singleton class every time (not a bean)
  • @Scope(value="request")
  • If the data needs to be shared but thread safe: https://www.baeldung.com/java-thread-safety
    • Stateless static methods (just takes an input)
    • Atomic objects, like AtomicInteger
    • Immutable variables (private final and use a getter)

notes.html:
on 1 CPU core -> concurrency only (swapping between threads/tasks) on N CPU cores -> concurrency and parallelism

models

thread per task

  • lots of threads may sit blocked waiting on I/O, consuming unnecessary memory
  • still high concurrency and cpu utilization (cpu does not get blocked by blocked thread), but when threads are blocked, new threads are spawned (keeping the blocked threads in memory)

async / event loop

  • a small number of threads stop working on the blocked task while it waits and pick up other work
  • re-allocate blocked threads to work on another task
  • ex: js event loop

benefits:

  • less memory per concurrent task
  • less thread/context-switch overhead
  • scales much better for I/O-heavy workloads

problem it solves:

  • waiting threads (even if CPU is not processing them) take up memory
  • scaling many waiting threads uses unnecessary memory due to thread memory overhead
  • synchronous I/O by definition makes the thread wait for I/O response
  • to solve that, we can make asynchronous I/O calls
  • issue: asynchronous by itself means we fire and forget, lose track of the response
  • what if we need/want to response tracked
  • that's where event loops are helpful

track the asynchronous threads to get response information without holding the thread blocked, causing many new threads to spawn to take on active work (even if it's not a CPU burden, it's a memory burden as new threads take memory)

Purpose: represent real world entities in the real world

Problem that OOP solves:

  • Procedural spaghetti code
  • One change can break many places
  • Functions with so many parameters

Encapsulation

  • For separation of concerns
  • Variables and methods related to an object lives in that object
  • Method can operate on the instance variables

Abstraction

  • Hide complexities
  • Simple interface
  • Reduce impact of change
    • Change to private methods do not leak to the outside

Inheritance

  • Generalize shared variables and methods
  • Reduce redundant code

Polymorphism

  • Help avoid long if/else switch/case
  • Helps with strategy pattern
  • Child class has a custom implementation

notes.html:
• L7 – Application: User-facing protocols (HTTP, gRPC, DNS)
  • L6 – Presentation: Encoding, compression, TLS
  • L5 – Session: Connection/session mgmt (mostly implicit today)
  • L4 – Transport: Data delivery (TCP, UDP)
  • L3 – Network: Routing (IP)
  • L2 – Data Link: Local network, frames (Ethernet, Wi-Fi)
  • L1 – Physical: Wires, radio, bits

protocols

On top of L7

  • REST (style)
    • Layer: L7
    • Runs on: HTTP → TCP
  • gRPC
    • Layer: L7
    • Runs on: HTTP/2 → TCP
    • backend to backend, streaming
  • WebSockets
    • Layer: L7
    • Runs on: HTTP (upgrade) → TCP
    • web to backend, live chat root, streaming

Application Layer (L7)

  • HTTP / HTTPS
    • Layer: L7
    • Runs on: TCP (HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2), UDP (HTTP/3 via QUIC)
  • WebRTC
    • Layer: L7
    • Runs on: UDP (SRTP/DTLS), TCP/HTTP for signaling
    • zoom call, streaming
  • DNS
    • Layer: L7
    • Runs on: UDP (default), TCP (large responses)
  • FTP
    • Layer: L7
    • Runs on: TCP
  • SMTP / IMAP / POP3
    • Layer: L7
    • Runs on: TCP

Security / Encoding (L6-ish)

  • TLS / SSL
    • Layer: L6 (conceptually)
    • Runs on: TCP (TLS), UDP (DTLS)

Transport Layer (L4)

  • TCP
    • Layer: L4
    • Runs on: IP
    • Reliable, ordered, congestion-controlled
  • UDP
    • Layer: L4
    • Runs on: IP
    • Fast, unordered, no guarantees
  • QUIC
    • Layer: L4-ish
    • Runs on: UDP
    • TCP + TLS + HTTP/3 semantics combined

Network Layer (L3)

  • IP (IPv4 / IPv6)
    • Layer: L3
    • Runs on: Ethernet / Wi-Fi
  • ICMP
    • Layer: L3
    • Runs on: IP (errors, ping)

Data Link (L2)

  • Ethernet
    • Layer: L2
    • Runs on: Physical media
  • Wi-Fi (802.11)
    • Layer: L2
    • Runs on: Radio
  • ARP
    • Layer: L2/3 bridge
    • Runs on: Ethernet

Common Stacks

  • REST API
    REST → HTTP → TCP → IP
  • gRPC
    gRPC → HTTP/2 → TCP → IP
  • WebSocket
    WS → HTTP → TCP → IP
  • HTTP/3
    HTTP/3 → QUIC → UDP → IP
  • WebRTC Media
    SRTP → UDP → IP

notes.html:
Interpreter = executes code as instructions step by step

  • runs in an env (process VM) that usually software simulator for machine to code run portably (the interpreter can take bytecode and map to pre-compiled C code for current machine) Compiler = instructions are bundled into machine-ready package (executable).
  • runs directly on cpu

CPython is a machine native (OSX, Linux, WIndows, ARM, x86, etc) compiled application that is a runtime interpreter for Python

  • it will compile the code into bytecode
  • then use Python VM (process VM) to execute the bytecode
    • by reading bytecode instructions and dispatching to C code
    • Containers VMs Hypervisor
    • VM - software to simulate machine
    • uses OS syscalls
YoYour .py source
      ->
  Python bytecode
      ->
  Python VM / bytecode evaluator
      ->
  CPython interpreter process
      ->
  Host OS (syscalls)
      ->
  Hardware (CPU)

Interpreter under the hood

  • it maps the bytecode operations to native C functions
  • and all those C functions (C Code) is already compiled into ARM or x86 machine code

  1. .py source
     "x = 2 + 3; print(x)"

  2. Python bytecode
     LOAD_CONST 5
     STORE_NAME x
     LOAD_NAME print
     LOAD_NAME x
     CALL 1

  3. CPython bytecode evaluator
     reads LOAD_CONST 5
     pushes Python int object 5 onto stack
       while (running) {
      instruction = next_bytecode();

      switch (instruction.opcode) {
          case LOAD_NAME:
              // C code to load a Python variable
              break;

          case BINARY_OP:
              // C code to perform Python addition
              break;

          case STORE_NAME:
              // C code to store a Python variable
              break;
	      }
	  }

  4. Precompiled CPython machine code
     CPU runs CPython's compiled code for:
     "push constant", "store variable", "call function"
     
     (precompiled c code at the time of Python install)

  5. OS syscall
     print(x) eventually asks OS:
     write stdout bytes: "5\n"

  6. Hardware
     CPU executes machine instructions
     terminal/display shows:
     5

Why interpreter?

to compile for different machines, requires different compilation methods

interpreter can allow for intermediate portable instruction set to be consumed and installed interpreter can run it natively on the machine. so now the compile to intermediate bytecode is the same across all machines, and each machine type can have it's own interpreter downloaded to execute the bytecode accordingly

notes.html:
WebFlux framework is a newer framework over MVC.

  • It provides asynchronous thread safe API calls out of the box
  • Use WebClient instead of the deprecated RestFramework

WebFlux follows the Reactive pattern which is a functional programming pattern

Examples

API Call

Write spring boot code for calling an API using webflux synchronously

package com.example.demo;

import org.springframework.web.reactive.function.client.WebClient;
import org.springframework.web.reactive.function.client.WebClient.ResponseSpec;

public class WebFluxClient {

    public static void main(String[] args) {

        WebClient webClient = WebClient.create("http://localhost:8080/api/v1");

        ResponseSpec responseSpec = webClient.get().uri("/data").exchange();

        responseSpec.bodyToMono(String.class).subscribe(System.out::println);
    }
}

Rest Controller

A simple rest controller with WebFlux

import reactor.core.publisher.Flux;
import reactor.core.publisher.Mono;

import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.DeleteMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.PathVariable;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/users")
public class MyRestController {

    private final UserRepository userRepository;

    private final CustomerRepository customerRepository;

    public MyRestController(UserRepository userRepository, CustomerRepository customerRepository) {
        this.userRepository = userRepository;
        this.customerRepository = customerRepository;
    }

    @GetMapping("/{userId}")
    public Mono<User> getUser(@PathVariable Long userId) {
        return this.userRepository.findById(userId);
    }

    @GetMapping("/{userId}/customers")
    public Flux<Customer> getUserCustomers(@PathVariable Long userId) {
        return this.userRepository.findById(userId).flatMapMany(this.customerRepository::findByUser);
    }

    @DeleteMapping("/{userId}")
    public Mono<Void> deleteUser(@PathVariable Long userId) {
        return this.userRepository.deleteById(userId);
    }

}
